## What changed

Notifications, so that a nineteen-step climb does not need you at the terminal.

**A delivery failure was being mistaken for a delivered message.** Telegram
answers a bad token with a perfectly successful HTTP request carrying 401 —
nothing throws, the promise resolves, and until now that counted as sent. With
a wrong token or chat id every notification across nineteen steps would have
vanished in silence: you wait for messages that will never arrive and never
learn why, which defeats the entire point of having them. Non-2xx replies are
now named, with the bot token and webhook URL redacted out of the message —
the token sits in the request URL, and these lines go to the system journal.

**Finding your Telegram chat id no longer means doing it by hand.** It used to
take `curl`, `grep` over JSON, and your bot token typed onto a command line
where `ps` can read it. With the token already in the config,
`gitlab-upgrade notify chat` waits for you to press Start in the bot chat and
answers *in that chat* with its id, which is where you are looking anyway. It
also prints it, and with `--yes` writes it to the config.

Three decisions worth stating. It never picks for you when several people have
written to the bot — silently choosing one is how upgrade reports end up going
to a stranger. The token comes only from the config, never a flag, because a
command-line argument is visible in `ps` to anyone on the machine. And a
webhook on the bot, which makes `getUpdates` impossible, is reported as its own
diagnosis rather than as "nobody wrote" — waiting there is pointless.

Both paths were verified against the live `api.telegram.org` through a real
SOCKS5 proxy, not only against stubs: the proxy logged
`CONNECT api.telegram.org:443`, and an invalid token came back as
`HTTP 401: Unauthorized` with the token itself nowhere in the output.

**The project's own linter could not see a syntax error.** `a ?? b || c`
without parentheses passed it and failed at runtime — "0 errors" was a lie.
Every file is parsed now, which was verified by breaking one on purpose.

**The PostgreSQL barrier was checked once, before the climb, and then never
again.** On a nineteen-step route the database version changes underneath you —
PostgreSQL 13 arrives with the 15.0 package, 14 with 17.0 — so an answer given
at the start is stale by step eight. With `--force` the run would have handed
apt a 16.3 package on PostgreSQL 12, in the middle of a multi-hour unattended
climb, which is the worst possible place to discover it. Every step now checks
the requirement for that step against the database as it is right then, and
stops cleanly before the step it cannot satisfy — before taking the backup,
because an hour spent backing up for a step that will not run is an hour
wasted. The state is saved, so `resume` continues once the database is up.

The remedy for a *deferred* barrier was also wrong, and a real machine proved
it: `gitlab-ctl pg-upgrade` on 13.12 answers "the latest version 12.6 is
already running, nothing to do". It can only reach the version the *installed*
package carries, and the version you need arrives with a package further along
the route. Advising it today was advising a no-op; the finding now says when
the upgrade becomes possible instead of naming a command that does nothing.
